## Website Designer in Pune: Why Your Logo Does Not Show in Google Search Results — The Favicon Rules, Sizes and Fixes Explained

Your logo does not appear beside your website name in Google results for one of a few reasons: the favicon is not declared in the home page's `<link>` tag, it is declared but Google has not yet re-crawled the home page, the image file is blocked or broken, it is not square, or Google has simply chosen not to show it. Google's own documentation says that "a favicon isn't guaranteed to appear in Google Search results" even when every guideline is met, so the goal is to remove every avoidable obstacle and then wait for a re-crawl. This guide is written for the owner of a business website in Pune or elsewhere in India who has noticed a grey globe where the logo should be, and for the designer or developer who has been asked to fix it. It sets out Google's published rules, the exact markup, how to produce files that survive being shrunk to a few pixels, how to check what Google sees, and what to put in a design brief so the problem does not come back after a redesign.

We rely on Google Search Central's "Define a favicon to show in search results" documentation throughout. Where something is our own judgement from building websites, we say so. We do not claim that a favicon improves rankings: Google does not say that, and we have no measurement that would support it. What a favicon does is make your result recognisable on a crowded page, which is a branding and trust matter rather than a ranking one.

## What a favicon is and where it appears

A favicon is the small square image that represents your site. Browsers show it in tabs and bookmarks. Google shows it next to the site name and URL in mobile and desktop search results. Because it sits beside every result you earn, it is the only part of your brand that appears in search before a click. A searcher scanning ten results for "website designer in Pune" will see ten site names; a clear mark beside yours helps a returning visitor spot you, and a blank globe makes a legitimate business look less established than it is. That is a judgement, not a measured effect, but it is why the fix is worth an hour of a designer's time.

Google's guidance applies to organic results. Logos in Google Ads follow different specifications, so do not expect a favicon change to alter how your paid listings look.

## The rules Google publishes

Google's documentation sets out the requirements plainly. We list them here and then explain what each means in practice.

**One favicon per hostname.** Google supports a favicon for a domain-level home page such as `https://example.com` and for a subdomain-level home page such as `https://news.example.com`. It does not support a subdirectory-level home page such as `https://example.com/news`. A favicon set on the root applies to the site and its subdirectories. In practice this means a business with a main site and a separate subdomain, for example a store at `shop.` or a blog at `blog.`, needs the tag on each hostname's home page if it wants each represented.

**The tag goes on the home page.** The documentation tells you to add a `<link>` tag to the header of your home page. Google reads it from there. Putting it on inner pages alone does not do the job.

**Crawlability.** Googlebot-Image must be able to crawl the favicon file, and Googlebot must be able to crawl the home page. Neither can be blocked. This is where many sites fail quietly, because a `robots.txt` rule written to keep crawlers out of an images or assets folder can also block the favicon.

**Shape and size.** The image must be square, a 1:1 aspect ratio, and at least 8 by 8 pixels. Google recommends more than 48 by 48 pixels so that it displays well on different surfaces.

**Formats.** Google lists BMP, GIF, ICO, PNG, JPEG, PPM and TIFF. In practice, almost every site uses PNG, ICO or SVG-adjacent workflows exported to PNG. Note that SVG is not in Google's list of supported formats in that documentation, so do not rely on an SVG-only favicon for Google's purposes even if browsers accept it for tabs.

**Representative of the brand.** The favicon should visually represent your brand so people can identify the site.

**A stable URL.** Google asks you not to change the favicon's URL frequently. Each change forces re-processing and delays the update.

**Appropriate content.** Google will not show favicons it deems inappropriate, and replaces them with a default icon if it finds such imagery. This is rarely an issue for a business, but it explains one cause of a default icon on a site whose files have been compromised.

**It can take time.** After you change the tag, Google must recrawl and process the home page. The documentation says this can take several days to several weeks, and that you can request indexing with the URL Inspection tool.

## The markup, exactly

The simplest correct implementation is one line in the `<head>` of the home page:

```html
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico">
```

Google documents these `rel` values as supported: `icon`, the standard value; `shortcut icon`, an older alternative that Google still supports; `apple-touch-icon`, which is friendly to iOS; and `apple-touch-icon-precomposed`, an alternative for earlier iOS versions. The `href` can be a relative path or an absolute URL, and the favicon does not have to live on your own domain, so a CDN address is acceptable.

A set that works well in practice, and that we would brief a developer to produce, is:

```html
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any">
<link rel="icon" type="image/png" sizes="192x192" href="/favicon-192x192.png">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
```

This is our own pattern rather than a Google requirement. The `.ico` file covers older browsers and the habit crawlers have of requesting `/favicon.ico` by default; the larger PNG gives Google a source well above the 48-pixel recommendation; and the touch icon serves iOS home-screen shortcuts. If your build tool already generates a manifest with larger icons for installable-site use, that is separate and does no harm.

One practical warning: if the tag points to a path that returns a redirect, a 404 or an HTML error page, Google will treat the favicon as unavailable. Open the exact `href` in a browser and confirm that it returns an image.

## Why a logo makes a poor favicon, and what to do instead

The most common design mistake is to shrink the full logo. A horizontal logo with a symbol and a company name is wide, so it either has to be padded into a square, leaving the mark tiny, or cropped. At 16 or 32 pixels, small lettering turns to mush. Google recommends more than 48 by 48 pixels as a source, but the same file is shown smaller in tabs, so it must survive both.

The approach that works is to design the favicon as its own asset:

1. **Use the symbol, not the wordmark.** If your logo has a distinctive mark, use only that. If it is only text, use one or two letters, such as an initial, in the brand typeface or colour.
2. **Fill the square.** Leave a small margin, but do not leave a quarter of the canvas empty. Empty space makes the mark smaller than it needs to be.
3. **Reduce detail.** Remove gradients, thin strokes and taglines. Test by viewing the file at 16 pixels on a real screen.
4. **Mind contrast.** Google results can appear on light or dark backgrounds depending on the user's settings. A pale mark on a transparent background can vanish in one of them. A solid brand-colour tile with a white or contrasting symbol is safer, and this is our judgement rather than a Google rule.
5. **Keep the original source.** Export from a vector master at the sizes you need rather than scaling a small PNG up.

A short worked example, illustrative only and not a client result: suppose a Pune dental clinic's logo is a tooth icon beside the words "Smile Care Dental Clinic, Kothrud". The favicon should be the tooth icon alone on a solid teal tile, exported at 512, 192, 48 and 32 pixels. Putting the clinic name into it would make it illegible at any size at which it is displayed.

## Why yours may not be showing: a diagnostic order

Work through these in order. Each step is cheap, and the earlier ones are the most common causes.

### 1. Is the tag on the home page?

View the source of your home page, not an inner page, and search for `rel="icon"`. If a theme, builder or plugin injects the tag only on certain templates, it may be missing on the home page. On WordPress, the site icon is set in the Customizer or site editor, and many themes output the tag only when it is set there. Check that someone has not uploaded a favicon through a plugin that is now disabled.

### 2. Does the file load?

Copy the `href` into the browser. You should see the image. If you see an error page, a login screen or a redirect, fix the path. Confirm the response is an image and not an HTML page returned with a 200 status, which is a classic soft-error pattern after a migration.

### 3. Is anything blocking it?

Read `robots.txt` at your domain root. Look for `Disallow` rules that cover the folder holding your icon, such as `/wp-content/` or `/assets/`, and check that Googlebot-Image is not disallowed. Also confirm the home page itself is not blocked. If you have recently tightened rules to manage AI crawlers, re-read them; our guide to [robots.txt and AI crawlers](/blog/web-development-company-pune-ai-crawlers-robots-txt-2026/) explains how to do that without cutting off Google's own bots.

### 4. Is it square and large enough?

Open the file's properties. A 100 by 60 image fails the 1:1 rule. An 8 by 8 file technically passes but is far below the recommended 48 pixels.

### 5. Is the format on Google's list?

Use PNG or ICO. If your only declared favicon is an SVG, add a PNG alongside it.

### 6. Has the URL changed recently?

Google asks you not to change it often. If your developer renames the file with each build, as some build tools do by appending a hash to the filename, every deployment restarts the process. Keep a stable path for the favicon even if other assets are fingerprinted.

### 7. Has Google had time to re-crawl?

Google's documentation says days to weeks. Use the URL Inspection tool on your home page to request indexing, which is the step Google itself names. Then wait. Do not change the file again during the wait, because each change resets the clock.

### 8. Have you set up Search Console correctly?

If your site is verified only as a URL-prefix property for one variant, for example `http://` or `www`, while the canonical home page is a different variant, you may be inspecting the wrong page. Our guide to [Search Console properties](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-search-console-platform-properties-2026/) explains how to set that up so that you see what Google sees.

### 9. Could the canonical home page be a different hostname?

If your site resolves on both `www` and non-`www`, Google shows the favicon of the version it treats as canonical. If your tag exists only on one, the result may show a default. Our article on [canonical URLs, www and HTTPS](/blog/web-development-company-pune-canonical-urls-duplicate-content-www-https-2026/) covers choosing and enforcing one version.

### 10. Is it still just a default?

If every box above is ticked and a few weeks have passed, you may be in the group Google's documentation describes when it says there is no guarantee. Google offers a feedback form for favicon problems, and says plainly that feedback does not guarantee individual action. Submit it once, do not keep tinkering, and accept that you have done what can be done.

## Platform notes

**WordPress.** Set the Site Icon in the Customizer or the site editor. Upload a large square image, and check WordPress's own on-screen guidance for the recommended size. Check the page source afterwards, because some page-builder themes ignore this setting and output their own tag. Our guide to [WordPress plugin audits](/blog/web-development-company-pune-wordpress-plugin-audit-abandoned-plugins-2026/) is relevant if more than one plugin claims to manage icons.

**Shopify.** The favicon is set in the theme settings, and you upload a square image. Use a large one, and check the home page source after saving.

**Custom-built sites, including React and Next-style builds.** The tag has to be present in the initial HTML the server returns, not added by JavaScript after load, because Google must find it when it processes the home page. Put the tag in the base HTML template. If you pre-render pages, confirm the pre-rendered home page contains the link tag.

**Multiple brands on one domain.** Because Google supports one favicon per hostname, one site cannot show different icons for different sections under subdirectories. If two brands need separate icons, they need separate hostnames.

## What to put in a design or redesign brief

A favicon is usually forgotten until launch, and a redesign is the moment it breaks. Add these lines to your brief:

- Deliver a favicon as a separate asset: a square PNG at 512 pixels, plus 192, 48 and 32 pixel exports, and an `.ico` file.
- State that the tag must be in the home page head in the server-delivered HTML.
- State that the file path must stay the same after launch and across deployments.
- Ask for a check of `robots.txt` to confirm the icon folder and Googlebot-Image are not blocked.
- Include the favicon in the pre-launch checklist and request indexing for the home page after launch.
- Ask that the 16-pixel and 32-pixel versions be viewed on a real phone and laptop and signed off by whoever owns the brand.

If you are moving to a new domain or changing hostnames at the same time, treat the favicon as part of the move plan, and read our article on [domain changes and redirect mapping](/blog/web-development-company-pune-domain-change-site-move-redirect-map-2026/) first.

## What a favicon will and will not do for you

It will make your result easier to recognise, give a consistent brand cue across tab, bookmark and search result, and remove the generic globe that can make a small business look unfinished. It will not, as far as anything Google publishes says, change your ranking. It will not appear instantly, and Google says it will not necessarily appear at all. We put this plainly because favicon work is sometimes sold as an SEO service with promised results. It is a small, worthwhile hygiene task, and it is best handled as part of a proper site build or maintenance plan rather than as a separate paid campaign.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why is my logo not showing in Google search results?

The usual causes are a missing or misplaced `<link rel="icon">` tag on the home page, a blocked or broken icon file, an image that is not square, or Google not yet having re-crawled the page. Google also says a favicon is not guaranteed to appear even when its guidelines are met.

### What size should a favicon be for Google?

Google requires a square image of at least 8 by 8 pixels and recommends more than 48 by 48 pixels so it displays well on different surfaces. A 192 or 512 pixel PNG source is a safe choice, though those larger sizes are our suggestion rather than a Google number.

### How long does it take for a new favicon to appear in Google?

Google's documentation says that after you change the tag, recrawling and processing the home page can take several days to several weeks. You can request indexing of the home page with the URL Inspection tool, and you should avoid changing the file again while you wait.

### Can I have a different favicon for each page or section?

No. Google supports one favicon per hostname, set from the domain-level or subdomain-level home page. A subdirectory home page is not supported, so separate icons would need separate subdomains or domains.

### Does a favicon help SEO?

Google does not say it is a ranking factor. Its value is in recognition and trust at the point where your result appears, not in rankings.

- Our own judgement is labelled as such: the markup set, the design advice on symbol versus wordmark and contrast, the platform notes and the brief checklist are practice, not Google statements.
